questions.prompt: Array a has 18 elements. Which reshape call works?

options.label: A
options.text: a.reshape(4, 5)

options.label: B
options.text: a.reshape(3, 6)

options.label: C
options.text: a.reshape(2, 8)

options.label: D
options.text: a.reshape(6, 4)

questions.explanation: The new shape has to hold exactly as many elements as you already have, with no cell left over and none missing, because reshape changes how the data is read without adding or dropping anything. Only 3×6 comes to exactly 18 cells. The 4×5 and 6×4 options ask for 20 and 24 cells, more than there are, so nothing would fill the surplus; 2×8 has only 16 cells, meaning two numbers would have to be left behind, which NumPy will not do on its own. All three stop with a ValueError rather than quietly trimming or padding.

questions.prompt: What does writing -1 for one dimension in reshape mean?

options.label: A
options.text: That dimension is dropped, so the result has one dimension fewer than the original

options.label: B
options.text: That dimension is read in reverse order, with the last element coming first

options.label: C
options.text: That dimension gets a length of exactly 1, just like adding a new axis

options.label: D
options.text: NumPy works out that dimension's length from the total element count and the other dimensions

questions.explanation: -1 is the slot you leave for NumPy to compute: given the total number of elements and the lengths of the other dimensions, the remaining length has only one possible answer, so arr.reshape(-1, 3) on 12 numbers gives a 4-row table. Because that answer has to be unique, -1 may appear in one dimension only - with two blanks the division has infinitely many solutions. It does not drop a dimension: reshape(-1, 3) still returns a two-dimensional array. It does not reverse anything either - reshape always takes the numbers in their flat order - and it does not force a length of 1; adding an axis of length 1 is the job of np.newaxis.

questions.prompt: What is the real difference between grid.ravel() and grid.flatten()?

options.label: A
options.text: ravel returns a view when the layout allows it, so writing to the result can change grid too, while flatten always copies into a new array

options.label: B
options.text: ravel flattens column by column and flatten flattens row by row, so the two results hold the numbers in a different order

options.label: C
options.text: ravel only accepts two-dimensional arrays while flatten accepts any number of dimensions; otherwise the results are the same

options.label: D
options.text: ravel returns a Python list while flatten returns a NumPy array, so the two results have different types

questions.explanation: Both flatten the array into a one-dimensional sequence in the same order - a whole row before moving down - so saying they flatten along different dimensions is wrong. The only thing that separates them is memory: ravel tries to return a view, reusing the very memory of grid, so assigning into an element of the result can change grid as well; flatten allocates new memory and copies into it, and the result lives independently. Both accept arrays of any number of dimensions, and both return a NumPy array rather than a list - for a list you have to call .tolist() on top.

questions.prompt: You run t = grid.T and then t[0, 0] = 99. What happens to grid?

options.label: A
options.text: grid is unchanged, because .T copies the data into a new memory layout

options.label: B
options.text: grid[0, 0] becomes 99 as well, because .T is a view onto the same memory

options.label: C
options.text: The program raises an error, because a transposed array cannot be written to

options.label: D
options.text: grid is unchanged, unless grid is square with as many rows as columns

questions.explanation: .T does not touch the data, it only changes how the existing memory is walked: what used to be read row by row is now read column by column. That is why np.shares_memory(grid, grid.T) returns True, and writing into the first cell of the transposed table writes straight into grid[0, 0]. Precisely because nothing is copied, .T is nearly free even on large arrays - if it copied into a new layout, transposing a few hundred megabytes would cost that much memory every single time. Writing into a view is perfectly legal and no error is raised, and whether the array is square makes no difference: the .T of a 2×3 table is a view just the same.

questions.prompt: Two tables both have 5 columns, one with 3 rows and one with 7 rows. How do you join them into a 10-row table?

options.label: A
options.text: np.concatenate([a, b], axis=1), because axis 1 is the axis that gathers data together

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot be done, because concatenate requires the two arrays to have identical shapes

options.label: C
options.text: np.concatenate([a, b], axis=0), and np.vstack([a, b]) gives the same result

options.label: D
options.text: np.hstack([a, b]), because it is the only way to join two tables with different row counts

questions.explanation: The dimension that has to grow is the row dimension, axis 0, so axis=0 is the answer, and np.vstack is the shortcut for that exact call. The only condition is that every other dimension match - here both tables have 5 columns, so the join is legal, which also shows that concatenate never demands identical shapes, only agreement on the dimensions it is not joining along. Choosing axis=1 would paste the tables side by side and require an equal number of rows, and 3 differs from 7, so it errors out. np.hstack is a horizontal join too, the same wrong direction.

questions.prompt: You have weights with 4 numbers and heights with 6, and you need a 4×6 table with the product of every pair. Which one is right?

options.label: A
options.text: weights * heights, letting broadcasting handle the pairing

options.label: B
options.text: np.concatenate([weights, heights]).reshape(4, 6)

options.label: C
options.text: weights.reshape(1, -1) * heights, turning weights into a row

options.label: D
options.text: weights[:, np.newaxis] * heights, turning weights into a column

questions.explanation: To get a table, one of the two arrays has to stand upright: weights[:, np.newaxis] has shape (4, 1), and meeting (6,) broadcasting pads that to (1, 6) and then stretches both length-1 axes, giving (4, 6) - one row per weight, one column per height. Multiplying weights * heights directly makes the broadcasting rule compare (4,) with (6,) at the last axis; the two differ and neither is 1, so it stops with an error. Turning weights into a row (1, 4) snags at the very same place, since the last axis is still 4 against 6. And concatenating the two arrays yields only 10 numbers, not enough for 24 cells, and they are not the product of any pair either.

lessons.title: Reproducible random numbers
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 49: Reproducible random numbers

theory.contentHtml:
You write a simulation and get an error rate of 4%. A colleague runs that exact file, gets 6%, and asks what you changed. Nobody changed anything - every run draws a different sequence of random numbers. The way to get both of you talking about the same thing is to build the generator from a fixed seed:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, size=5))
print(np.round(rng.random(3), 3).tolist())
[1 5 4 3 3]
[0.697, 0.094, 0.976]

default_rng(42) creates a generator, and from that generator you call integers for whole numbers in a range (the upper bound is never drawn, so 1, 7 means die faces 1 through 6), random for floats between 0 and 1, and normal for numbers from a normal distribution.

Same seed, same sequence

A seed does not make the numbers any less random. It only decides where the generator starts, so two generators built from the same seed produce identical sequences, on every machine:

import numpy as np

first = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(loc=10, scale=2, size=4)
second = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(loc=10, scale=2, size=4)
print(np.round(first, 2).tolist())
print(np.array_equal(first, second))
[10.0, 10.6, 9.45, 8.22]
True

That is what lets you replay a suspicious simulation exactly as it happened while you dig into it; and when you compare two approaches, you know the gap comes from the algorithm and not from drawing a different sequence.

Why default_rng and not np.random.seed

Older code tends to call np.random.seed(42) and then np.random.randint(...). That seeds one generator shared by the entire program: a library you happen to call draws from it too, so a single extra line somewhere else shifts your sequence for no visible reason. default_rng returns a generator of your own - you hold it, nobody else touches it. Since NumPy 1.17 this is the recommended style for new code.

Every random number in this lesson, and in the rest of the course, comes from default_rng with the seed spelled out in the exercise.

lessons.title: Sampling and shuffling
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 51: Sampling and shuffling

theory.contentHtml:
You have a customer list and need to call 3 of them for a survey, picked at random so the choice isn't biased. rng.choice does that, and the replace argument decides whether the same person can be picked twice:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
customers = np.array(["c01", "c02", "c03", "c04", "c05"])
print(rng.choice(customers, size=3, replace=False))
print(rng.choice(customers, size=5, replace=True))
['c03' 'c02' 'c04']
['c01' 'c05' 'c05' 'c02' 'c02']

A survey needs replace=False - nobody gets called twice. Resampling to estimate confidence (bootstrap) is the opposite case: there replace=True is exactly what you want.

A new array, or shuffled in place

When you need to shuffle a whole list instead of picking a few items, there are two functions, and they differ in whether they touch the original array:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
order = np.arange(6)
shuffled = rng.permutation(order)
print(shuffled)
print(order)
rng.shuffle(order)
print(order)
[2 5 4 1 3 0]
[0 1 2 3 4 5]
[3 5 0 2 1 4]

permutation returns a new array and leaves the input untouched. shuffle shuffles the input array itself and returns None - writing order = rng.shuffle(order) wipes out your data, and it is the most common mistake with this function.

Shuffle the indices so pairs stay together

Machine learning data usually lives in two parallel arrays, features and labels, where row i of one belongs to row i of the other. Shuffling each array on its own breaks that pairing. The right way is to shuffle the index sequence, then use that one sequence for both arrays:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
features = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60])
labels = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0])
order = rng.permutation(features.size)
train, test = order[:4], order[4:]
print(features[train], labels[train])
print(features[test], labels[test])
[40 20 50 60] [1 1 1 0]
[30 10] [0 0]

Cutting the index sequence into two pieces splits the data into a training part and a test part, with every label still attached to its own row.

  • The row order is shuffled in one single pass with a random generator built from seed, shuffling the index sequence 0 to n - 1 - do not shuffle each array separately.
  • The training set has as many rows as the integer part of n * train_ratio. The rows that come first after the shuffle belong to the training set, the rest belong to the test set.
  • Return 4 arrays in order: training features, training labels, test features, test labels.

features = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80])
labels = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0])
x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test = split_dataset(features, labels, 42, 0.75)

[40 50 30 80 70 20] [1 1 0 0 1 1]
[60 10] [0 0]

The first line is the training set (6 rows), the second is the test set (2 rows). The value 40 sits at position 3 of features and its label is labels[3] - still 1 after the shuffle.

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication and solving systems
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 53: Matrix multiplication and solving systems

theory.contentHtml:
Two two-dimensional arrays, one asterisk, and a result that isn't what many people expect:

import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([[10, 0], [0, 10]])
print(a * b)
print(a @ b)
[[10  0]
 [ 0 40]]
[[10 20]
 [30 40]]

* multiplies each cell by the cell in the same position, true to NumPy's element-wise style. @ is the one that does matrix multiplication in the linear-algebra sense (for the two 2D matrices in this lesson, np.dot gives the same result). With two square matrices of the same shape like the example above, confusing the signs is especially dangerous: both operations run but return different results. Rectangular matrices do not have that coincidence - @ works only when the left column count equals the right row count.

The dimensions have to line up

In X @ Y, the number of columns in X must equal the number of rows in Y; the result has the rows of X and the columns of Y. A familiar example is a quantity table times a unit-price table:

import numpy as np

quantities = np.array([[2, 1, 3], [0, 4, 1]])
unit_prices = np.array([50, 20, 10])
print(quantities.shape, unit_prices.shape)
print(quantities @ unit_prices)
(2, 3) (3,)
[150  90]

Each row is an order, each column an item: 3 columns line up with 3 unit prices, producing 2 order totals. If they don't line up, NumPy stops immediately with ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch... - read the two shapes in the message and you know which side is off.

Going the other way: solving a system of equations

If you know the quantities and the totals and need the unit prices, that is solving a system of equations. np.linalg.solve takes the coefficient matrix and the right-hand side:

import numpy as np

counts = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])
totals = np.array([80.0, 90.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(counts, totals).tolist())
[30.0, 20.0]

Two receipts: 2 of item A + 1 of item B cost 80, 1 of A + 3 of B cost 90 - so A is 30 and B is 20. This function needs a square matrix and a system with a unique solution; a singular system (where two equations are really the same one) raises LinAlgError.

lessons.title: Comparing floats correctly
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 55: Comparing floats correctly

theory.contentHtml:
An automated test comes back red, yet the two numbers look identical. Try it straight in Python:

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(0.1 + 0.2)
False
0.30000000000000004

Computers store floats in binary with a finite number of digits, and 0.1 in binary is an infinitely repeating number - just like 1/3 in decimal. So 0.1 is already an approximation once stored, adding two approximations gives another one, and it differs from the stored 0.3 at the seventeenth digit. This happens in every language, not just Python or NumPy.

Use allclose instead of ==

Because of that, two results that are mathematically correct can still differ in the last digit. NumPy ships two comparisons with a tolerance:

import numpy as np

expected = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
computed = np.array([0.05 + 0.05, 0.1 + 0.1, 0.1 + 0.2])
print(computed == expected)
print(np.isclose(computed, expected))
print(np.allclose(computed, expected))
[ True  True False]
[ True  True  True]
True

isclose compares cell by cell and returns a boolean array; allclose returns one True/False value for the whole array. The default tolerance is around one part in a billion, wide enough for rounding error and still tight enough to catch a real bug. Need it tighter or looser, adjust rtol and atol.

== on an array gives you an array

Look at the first line of the output above: computed == expected doesn't give one answer, it gives a boolean array. If you write if computed == expected:, Python raises ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous - it cannot decide on its own whether an array of several elements counts as true or false. To get a single answer, wrap it in .all() (every cell is True) or .any() (at least one cell is True).

And as you saw in module 4: nan is not equal to itself, so nan == nan is False and np.isnan(value) is the right way to ask. np.allclose likewise treats two nan values as different unless you turn on equal_nan=True.

lessons.title: NumPy arrays in pandas and matplotlib
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 56: NumPy arrays in pandas and matplotlib

theory.contentHtml:
Real work rarely starts from a hand-written array. It starts with a CSV file read into pandas, and it ends with a chart. NumPy sits between those two ends, and it also sits underneath both libraries, so data moves back and forth with no extra step:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["hanoi", "danang", "hcmc"], "revenue": [120.5, 65.25, 240.0]})
revenue = df["revenue"].to_numpy()
print(type(revenue).__name__)
print(revenue.sum())
print(np.round(revenue / revenue.sum() * 100, 1).tolist())
ndarray
425.75
[28.3, 15.3, 56.4]

A DataFrame column is a Series, and .to_numpy() (or .values, the older spelling) turns it into the NumPy array you already know. Everything you learned in this course - element-wise arithmetic, boolean masks, aggregating along an axis - carries over unchanged. The other direction works too: pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=[...]) builds a table from a two-dimensional array.

Plotting straight from an array

matplotlib takes NumPy arrays directly, with no conversion to a list:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

month = np.arange(1, 7)
revenue = np.array([120, 135, 150, 128, 162, 175])
plt.plot(month, revenue, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("month")
plt.ylabel("revenue")
plt.show()
print(revenue.mean())
print(revenue.max() - revenue.min())
145.0
55

Hit Run and the chart appears right below the output panel, with the two printed numbers beside it. This is a habit worth keeping: the picture for the shape, the numbers to check it - eyes misread a gap on a chart very easily, especially when the axis doesn't start at 0.

That covers the NumPy you need for everyday work. When you move on to pandas, you will find that most DataFrame operations are the NumPy operations you just learned, wearing column names.

lessons.title: Quiz NumPy in real work
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 58: Quiz NumPy in real work

questions.prompt: Why should you build the random generator from a fixed seed when running a simulation?

options.label: A
options.text: Because only with a seed are the numbers truly random; without one NumPy returns nothing but identical values

options.label: B
options.text: Because the same seed reproduces the same sequence, so rerunning reproduces the result for debugging and comparison

options.label: C
options.text: Because a seed makes number generation faster, saving time when simulating millions of draws

options.label: D
options.text: Because a seed limits the range of values produced, avoiding numbers so large they break the computation

questions.explanation: The seed decides where the generator starts, so two runs with the same seed produce exactly the same sequence on every machine. That is what lets a colleague rerun your file and get your numbers, what lets you replay a run that looks suspicious, and what tells you, when comparing two algorithms, that the gap comes from the algorithm and not from drawing a different sequence. A seed makes the numbers neither more nor less random - drop it and they are still distributed the same way, they just differ from run to run; they certainly aren't all identical. It also has nothing to do with generation speed, and even less with limiting the range of values: the range lives in the arguments to integers or random, not in the seed.

questions.prompt: How do rng.permutation(order) and rng.shuffle(order) differ?

options.label: A
options.text: permutation only accepts numeric arrays, while shuffle accepts both numeric and string arrays

options.label: B
options.text: shuffle keeps the order but changes the element values, while permutation does the opposite

options.label: C
options.text: The two give identical results for the same seed, they are just two names that read differently

options.label: D
options.text: permutation returns a new array and leaves the input untouched, while shuffle shuffles in place and returns None

questions.explanation: The difference lies in whether the function touches the original array. permutation gives you a new array and leaves the input exactly as it was, which suits you when the original data is still needed; shuffle shuffles in place and returns nothing, so order = rng.shuffle(order) assigns None right over the array it just shuffled - the most common mistake with this function. Both only rearrange the order and change no element's value, so there is no version that keeps the order and changes values. Both also accept every kind of array, string arrays included, and because they treat the original array differently they cannot stand in for each other.

questions.prompt: a and b are two two-dimensional arrays of the same shape. What does a * b produce?

options.label: A
options.text: An array of the same shape, where each cell is the product of the two cells at that position in a and b

options.label: B
options.text: The matrix product from linear algebra, that is, exactly the result of a @ b

options.label: C
options.text: A single number, the sum of the products of each pair of cells at the same position

options.label: D
options.text: A ValueError, because multiplying two two-dimensional arrays requires @

questions.explanation: * stays true to NumPy's element-wise style: every cell is multiplied by the cell at the same position in the other array, and the result has the same shape as the inputs. Matrix multiplication is the job of @ (or np.dot), and for [[1, 2], [3, 4]] * [[10, 0], [0, 10]] the two operations give completely different results. The dangerous part is that when the two arrays are square and have the same shape, both * and @ run smoothly, with no ValueError to warn you - the wrong number simply travels on into everything that follows. For two rectangular arrays of the same shape, * still works, but @ works only when the left column count equals the right row count. As for collapsing the result into a single number, that takes one more aggregation step, such as (a * b).sum(); the multiplication sign does not do it by itself.

questions.prompt: You write X @ Y where X has shape (3, 4). What shape must Y have for the multiplication to work?

options.label: A
options.text: (3, 4) - the two arrays must have the same shape to be multiplied

options.label: B
options.text: (3, 2) - Y must have as many rows as X has rows

options.label: C
options.text: (4, 2) - Y must have as many rows as X has columns

options.label: D
options.text: Any shape at all, NumPy broadcasts to make the dimensions fit

questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication pairs the columns of the left array with the rows of the right one, so the condition is that X has as many columns as Y has rows: (3, 4) @ (4, 2) works and gives a result of shape (3, 2). That is why (3, 4) is invalid for Y - equal or broadcast-compatible shapes are what element-wise * needs, not what @ needs. (3, 2) is wrong too: it lines rows up against rows, while the operation needs the columns on the left to match the rows on the right, so Y would have to have 4 rows. For the two-dimensional matrices in this question, the two multiplication dimensions must line up and broadcasting cannot repair a mismatch, so NumPy stops with a ValueError. With arrays of more than two dimensions, @ can still broadcast the leading batch dimensions, but the final two matrix dimensions follow this same rule.

questions.prompt: Why compare two floating-point results with np.allclose rather than ==?

options.label: A
options.text: Because == cannot be applied to float arrays; NumPy raises a dtype error the moment you compare

options.label: B
options.text: Because floating-point arithmetic carries rounding error, so two results that are mathematically equal still differ in the last digit

options.label: C
options.text: Because np.allclose runs considerably faster than == on arrays with millions of elements

options.label: D
options.text: Because == only compares the integer part of a float and ignores everything after the decimal point

questions.explanation: Floats are stored in binary with a finite number of digits, and 0.1 in binary repeats forever, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004 and comparing it with 0.3 using == gives False. np.allclose compares against a small tolerance, so it ignores a gap of that size while still catching a real discrepancy. == works perfectly well on float arrays and raises no error of any kind - it compares the decimal part in full, and it is precisely because it compares down to the last digit that it is too strict here. Speed is not the reason either: allclose does more work than ==, not less.

questions.prompt: You have a pandas DataFrame df and want to compute with NumPy and then draw a chart. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: You have to write the DataFrame out to a CSV file and read it back with NumPy to get an array to compute on

options.label: B
options.text: matplotlib only accepts Python lists, so arrays must be converted to lists before plotting

options.label: C
options.text: pandas and NumPy cannot share data; you have to copy value by value with a loop

options.label: D
options.text: df["col"].to_numpy() gives a NumPy array, and that array goes straight into plt.plot

questions.explanation: NumPy sits underneath both pandas and matplotlib, so data moves between them without any intermediate step: df["col"].to_numpy() (or .values, the older spelling) returns a NumPy array, and plt.plot(x, y) takes an array directly, with no conversion to a list. So there is no reason to write out a CSV and read it back - that round trip is slow and loses dtypes. Nor do you need a loop copying value by value, which is the slowest and most error-prone of the three wrong options. The reverse direction is built in as well: pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=[...]) builds a table from a two-dimensional array.
